No new route, no modal, no trip to the workshop. Safety contract: the confirm line names the exact file and key before you press (\"File to fix `capabilities/pay.md` · This sentence is in the description\"), **cancel changes 0 files** (and a second press is required when you have typed something), the save locks in the pressed frame so double-clicks write once, and `expected_mtime` means a concurrent human/agent edit is never silently overwritten — the row says so and reloads, and the retry merges (their keys survive, only this one line is added). The write target is `resolveNodeDocument(node).ownSlug` — the same single source of truth the workshop uses, so a concept without its own document never gets someone else's file written to.\n- **Similar names — are they the same?** (duplicate suspects) — concept pairs whose names/slug/kind/domain/neighbours overlap heavily, top 3 with the shared words as evidence, the overlap percent, a map deeplink to the node worth keeping, and a per-pair `merge_concepts` dry-run handoff. The score is a mirror of the MCP engine's `similar_nodes`, locked by `tests/contract/duplicate-pairs.contract.test.ts`, so screen and agent never name a different pair. Only nodes that own a vault document are considered (a node born from another doc's `elements:` ref has no file to merge). **0 suspects renders no section** — an empty \"no duplicates\" card is ink without a decision.\n- Queue sections show 3 rows each plus their total; the rest is the agent handoff's job (scroll contract).\n\n#### Tab 2 — Configuration Inventory\n- **Hero census** (`InsightsHeroCensus`) — concepts / relations / health facts (orphan count, cycle count, domain-membership rate, evidence-linked rate)\n- **Kind census** card — kind → glyph + bar + count, tallest bar highlighted\n- **Domain capacity** card — domain → bar (capability/element sub-counts), hidden when there are no domains\n\n#### Tab 3 — Connections\n- **Relation breakdown** — every edge type as a bar row with a `TopologyV2TraceMark` (solid=containment, dashed=depends/relates) + count + percent of total; empty vault gets a \"connect them on the map\" hint\n- **Hubs** — top nodes by degree: kind glyph + title + relative bar + degree, map deeplink per row, \"top N / M total\" folded into the single footnote line\n\n#### Tab 4 — Boundaries\n- **Domain coupling** — a domain×domain **heat grid** (rows send, columns receive; the diagonal is inside-one-domain connections in neutral). Cell shade is a 4-step indigo alpha ladder and every non-zero cell keeps its number, so the card never speaks in colour alone. Picking a cell opens that pair's relation-type counts and real example edges (map deeplinks) in a slot that is reserved whether or not anything is selected. Top 6 domains by cross activity; beyond that the footnote says \"top N of M domains\" and how many cross links fall outside the grid. Same `computeDomainCouplingMatrix` output as MCP `domain_matrix` — no new calculation.\n- **Boundary pressure** — per-domain inside vs cross ratio; a high cross share signals a leaking boundary\n- Cold start (fewer than 2 domains or no cross edges) shows one explicit empty state **with a next step** (map editor link) instead of a misleading table\n\n#### Tab 5 — Freshness\n- **Domain freshness heatstrip** — one row per domain, a week-by-week heat strip (neutral ramp, current week in indigo) built from real vault `updatedAt` values (`FRESHNESS_WINDOW_WEEKS`); domains with no dated docs are excluded from the stale count rather than counted as stale (\"unknown\" ≠ \"old\"); stale domains get a dashed \"stale\" tag\n- **Recent updates** — most recently touched nodes with kind glyph, domain, and ISO date; footer shows total stale-domain count\n\n#### Bottom handoff row (`InsightsHandoffRow`, always visible)\n- One copyable `query_ontology(...)` chain per active tab — the tab's question translated into the agent's execution order (connections → `centrality` then `blast_radius`; boundaries → `domain_matrix` then `match_edges`)\n\nEmpty state (0 nodes): link to `/docs` (open vault).\n\n---\n\n### `/topology?workbench=edit` — contextual meaning editor and change review\n\n- A selected node keeps its map context while its compact inspector swaps, at the\n  same anchor, into `MeaningEditorPanel`. There is no second right dock and no\n  separate review route.\n- One edit handles **one relation**. The user chooses type, target, and rationale,\n  or removes that existing relation from the same review path;\n  `depends_on` requires a rationale. Invalid `is_a` and containment target kinds\n  are filtered before selection.\n- The real map draws a dashed directional preview between the live endpoint\n  coordinates. This overlay never enters the force graph, so it cannot pull nodes\n  or change graph statistics. A density-hidden target is temporarily rendered at\n  its real coordinate and label. Confirming crossfades the same mark to solid,\n  then the local writer applies the reviewed frontmatter arrays with `expectedMtime`.\n- INDEX folds only during `workbench=edit` and restores after close. The responsive\n  contract keeps at least 480px of map between left chrome and editor from 1024px\n  upward; below `lg`, the editor is the single centered sheet above the tab bar.\n- New concept creation uses `workbench=create`. It no longer calls `createDoc`\n  from the first button press: the generated UID, slug, kind, display labels,\n  domain, and authorship fields are shown in `OntologyChangeReview`, and only\n  \"Confirm and write\" creates the file.\n- ACP keeps read tools frictionless. Every Atlas write tool pauses the same\n  conversation on a typed change card, hides `allow_always`, and resumes only on\n  `allow_once`; rejection is `reject_once`. The tool-mode policy is checked against\n  the generated `tools/list` surface so a new tool fails closed as a write.\n- Batch writers preserve and display every requested row in protocol order. The\n  review accordion selects one exact item at a time for the map preview, while\n  allow/reject applies honestly to the whole batch; the first item is never used\n  as a stand-in for hidden rows.\n- `/ontology/studio` and `/ontology/edit` remain only as compatibility addresses.\n  `node/mode/edit/via/review` are translated to `p/workbench/edit` on `/topology`.\n\n<details>\n<summary>Retired Compass Stage details (historical reference)</summary>\n\nThe following behavior described the removed Studio UI. It is retained only to\nexplain old screenshots and decisions; none of it is a current destination.\n\n- This is the **write screen** that fills in a concept's description and relationships. It places the node currently being edited large and centered on the screen, fixing the direction for each relationship type: up = parent concept (is_a), down = what this concept contains (contains), right = what this concept depends on (depends), left = similar concepts (relates). Directions must always remain constant so users do not need to re-read them every time. It opens from the \"Workshop\" in the left vertical menu. **There is only one screen, differing only in how much is filled, with no mode-selection tabs.**\n- **Enhancing existing nodes**: Opens an existing node (specified via a `?node=<id>` link; if unspecified, it automatically selects the capability with the most relationships) to fill in missing relationships. Already-filled relationships are drawn as indigo solid lines with small cards at their ends, while still-empty relationships are drawn as **empty spaces** with dashed lines (these are empty cells with only lines, not decorative icons). A \"Start filling here\" prompt is attached to only one of them.\n- **Creating new nodes (`?mode=create`)**: Opens the same screen entirely blank — a draft card for kind/name/domain/definition and empty relationship slots in four directions. Before saving, it separately notifies the user of \"1 new node, N relationships.\" If the name is similar to an existing node, the user can choose between \"Open existing node\" and \"Create anyway.\" However, if the kind and name match so closely that the file slug also overlaps, only \"Open existing node\" remains available; saving, save-previews, and change-previews are all blocked. The name input field is linked to this warning so screen readers announce it as well. Results are previewed in real-time while typing.\n- **Files change, not just the screen**: Filling an empty relationship slot writes directly to the frontmatter relationship list of the actual `.md` file (`localVault.updateFrontmatter`). In read-only vaults (e.g., samples), it instead copies a **bundle of MCP commands** for the AI agent to the clipboard. The target to connect with is selected from the list that appears immediately at that spot or created via \"Create new.\"\n- **Concepts without their own files are asked first**: Many concepts in the vault exist only because other documents listed their names in relationship lists, meaning they lack their own `.md` file (in this repository's vault, 198 out of 294). Since relationships are stored within a concept's file, one must create a file first to link relationships to such concepts. Because creating new files on the user's disk is something the user has never explicitly requested, **the system shows the file path to be created and asks for confirmation once** at the moment of saving. If cancelled, no files change (written content remains as a draft). If confirmed, a document containing both the relationships and the **path already pointed to by existing documents** is generated in a single write operation. If the kind cannot be determined, it does not arbitrarily decide but lets the user choose. In read-only vaults, it provides an MCP command bundle including `add_concept`.\n- **Enabled actual saving of parent concepts (is_a)**: \"What kind of thing is this node a kind of?\" was the most frequently empty item in the vault. Therefore, we added the `broader` key (the name used in SKOS standards) to the frontmatter and actually added it to graph calculations, schemas (mcp/cli), and gates so all components recognize this key. When filled, the dashed line becomes a solid line.\n- **How to show how much is filled**: Displayed via the borders of the four sides of the central card (dashed for empty sides, solid for filled sides). Below that is an easy-to-understand explanation (\"Filled 2 out of 4\"), and in the top-left corner is a small compass icon indicating what to do next. Game-style displays like percentage pie charts, levels, or grades are not used.\n- **Separated two seemingly similar questions (2026-07-28)**: The top button row is for selecting the node's **kind**, and the relationship slot in the up (↑) direction is for recording the **`broader` relationship**, i.e., \"is a sub-concept of which concept.\" These are different facts. Therefore, the button row has a visible single-word label \"Kind / Kind\" connected via `aria-labelledby`. The English question in the upper relationship slot is `What is this node a kind of?` — the previous phrase `What kind of thing is this node?` was corrected because it literally read as asking \"the kind of this node.\"\n- **Does not open below 1024px width and explains why (2026-07-28)**: This screen consists of a fixed-width card and relationship slots placed around its perimeter, making it unworkable on narrow screens (the installed app has a minimum width of `minWidth 1040`, so such widths do not appear at all, and the Workshop is excluded from mobile bottom tab bars). Links entering in `<lg` width from three sources (\"Edit Relationships\" in node details, Insights, Document frontmatter) now receive a single card explaining **why** (1024px width is required and it opens immediately when the window is widened) and **where to go** (Map · Desktop app). The Workshop screen itself is not drawn, nor does the first-visit guide appear on it — because introducing a non-existent screen would be a lie.\n- **Design**: Follows the same rules as the rest of the app — achromatic + one indigo + using only `--color-*` tokens. Amber (orange) is used solely as a signal for \"places that should naturally be filled but are empty.\" **Glow · gradients · gems · particles · gold are prohibited** (the previously existing game-style exception was abolished on 2026-07-24). The only motion is a change in opacity and color over 200ms when filling a relationship slot, and even that stops under the `prefers-reduced-motion` setting. All screen text uses plain language (\"What kind of thing is this node?\").\n\n</details>\n\n### `/ontology/edit` and `/ontology/studio` — compatibility redirects\n\nBoth old addresses now use `OntologyEditRedirectPage` to translate legacy\n`?node=`, `?mode=create`, and `?edit=` values into `/topology` workbench state.\nThe routes remain in the static export so old bookmarks do not 404; neither is\na navigation destination or a product screen.\n\n\n---\n\n### `/projects` — Project list (rebuilt 2026-07-18)\n\nRebuilt against RATIO-SYSTEM (1600px shared container). Therefore, the most prominent things on the screen are **the list of changed concepts and the \"Leave\" button** pair; everything else is either evidence for that judgment or merely the top/bottom borders of the screen.\n\nThe screen layout splits into two stages. First, **is this screen even in a state to do work** (`data-stage`) — if the browser can't run git or the vault hasn't been selected yet, it stops here. If it can work, it then splits by **whether there is something to decide now** (`data-shape`).\n\n#### State where work cannot start yet (`web` · `no-vault` · `not-initialized` · `loading` · `error`)\n- These states are all drawn in **the same size, same position** (`--git-setup-measure`\n  one 520px cell, centered on screen). If the width changes per stage, users feel like they're jumping to different pages every time\n- Shows what to do in one line: Open app → select folder → start recording.\n  Registering a remote repository is optional so it's not included in this line. No additional menus or decorative links here\n- In the browser, `Get App` is the primary button, and copying CLI commands for terminal use is secondary\n\n#### State with uncommitted changes (`decide`)\n- Left: One line of status totals at the top, then **file rows grouped by kind**\n  (status symbols `+ ~ − →` · folder names larger · how many lines added/removed). Clicking a row shows changed lines from that document on the right\n- Non-concept files (`.gitignore`, etc.) are **collapsed by default** — they go into the commit but aren't things humans need to judge. The number of collapsed lines is shown numerically so it's not hidden\n- Bottom fixed bar: Indigo-filled `Leave N items` button → confirmation step (preview of the actual commit title line + whether to push remotely, default off). Text explaining what is being recorded is also here — because files are actually written here\n- Right: Area showing evidence — `Changed lines` (file-by-file +/- lines with git internal notation removed) and `Previous steps` (previous commits). **Drawn only when there is content to show**\n- The width for splitting into 2 columns is `xl` (1280). Making it 2 columns at 1024 compresses the list and cuts off concept names\n\n#### State with nothing to leave (`recall`)\n- Does not split into 2 columns. A single-screen view where **the previous commit list is the body** (`--git-single-measure`)\n- What's in one commit line: how recent · simple summary (`Added 3 · Modified 2`) · author · short hash. Expanding shows full hash · ISO format time · **original commit title** (record needed for later tracking)\n- The primary button position remains inactive (`All left`). If the button disappears entirely based on state, users have to figure out what to press next every time\n\n#### Only simple language on screen\n- Commit titles automatically created by Atlas (`ontology snapshot: +3 concepts, …`) are converted to human language when shown on screen. Conversely, manually written commits or those made by other tools are left as-is since the original text is already human language (`describeSnapshotSubject`)\n- Git's internal notation (`diff --git` · `index <sha>..<sha>` ·\n  `@@ -a,b +c,d @@`) is not exposed on screen. However, a dashed line is **left** for skipped sections — hiding the fact that it was skipped makes that diff a lie\n\n#### Nothing is written until the user clicks\nWhen the screen first opens, only read-only tools are called (`git_status` / `git_diff` / `git_history`). Tools that change something (`git_init` · `git_set_remote` · `git_snapshot`) are executed only when the user presses their button (`onClick`).\n\n### `/agents` — Agent (new 2026-08-20, catalog 90)\n\n**One sentence on what this screen does**: **Get · install · attach · fix · and start conversation with** the AI coding tool on this computer.\n\n- **List** — Tools actually verified on this device are shown first, others are collapsed.\n- **Connection check** — Re-evaluate eight steps (does tool exist · can it launch · does it ask outside folder · is downloaded item intact · app-side settings · credential link · old login records · login). **Fixable things are fixed right there.** For unfixable ones, write what the human needs to do.\n- **App-specific installation** — Downloads Node and tools only inside the app folder. Fixes versions, and after downloading Node, **compares hashes** (if mismatched, delete and stop). Shows the original text before executing anything. Progress and completion remain on screen — even if you close and reopen the window.\n- **Reconnection** — Deletes only what the app created and recreates it. This is not \"logout\": this app has no app-side login, and links to the login the user did in the terminal, using it as-is.\n\n**Why it came out of settings**: Settings is **where you choose values**, and this is **an operational task with progress state**. A modal blocks the background and owns Esc, preventing you from seeing the map while receiving 52MB. **API Keys and workspaces remain in settings** — the former has a \"Path Freezing\" decision on 2026-08-16 (promoting destination is itself an emphasis), and the latter's axis answered by vault is different.\n\n**On the web**: The screen still appears, but states why it can't do what the browser can't (launching programs on this computer) along with the reason. It's not \"Connection unavailable\" — MCP is **attached to the folder**, not the screen, so web users are also connected (catalog 2026-08-01).\n\n## 3. MCP server (current runtime inventory)\n\nAI agents read/write the same vault as humans. Two ways to get the server running, and only two:\n\n| Channel | How the agent starts it | What the user does |\n|---|---|---|\n| **Installed desktop app** (primary; macOS 2026-07-27, Windows beta 2026-08-01) | The app ships a compiled MCP server inside its own bundle (`Ontology Atlas.app/Contents/MacOS/ontology-atlas-mcp` on macOS, `ontology-atlas-mcp.exe` beside the Windows executable). The agent client spawns that binary directly, so it keeps serving while the app is closed. | Open the vault folder in the app and press **Connect agent**. The app writes `.mcp.json` / `.codex/config.toml` with the bundled binary's absolute path and the vault's real path already filled in — no terminal, no Node, no install step. |\n| **Source checkout** (fallback) | `node <checkout>/mcp/src/index.js` with `OATLAS_VAULT` set. | Clone the repo, then either paste the config or let `node <checkout>/cli/src/index.mjs init` / `agent-setup --write` write it. |\n\nnpm publishing is retired (`docs/DECISIONS.md`, 2026-07-27) — there is no `npx` channel.\n\n**Connecting a project to its code (2026-08-04).** `connect_project_source`\n(CLI `connect-source`) binds one project node to the local folder holding the\ncode it describes, measures it, and writes the source receipt that\n`agent_brief` reports. Omit the folder and it infers one — the git repository\nenclosing the vault, otherwise the nearest ancestor carrying a project\nmanifest — then tells you how many of the ontology's declared `path:` claims\nactually exist inside it before anything is written. `confirm: true` binds;\n`disconnect_project_source` (CLI `disconnect-source`) undoes it. Each fallback command has a 15s default timeout, configurable with `--fallback-timeout-ms N` or `OATLAS_AGENT_FALLBACK_TIMEOUT_MS=N`, and timeout rows report `timedOut:true` for fail-closed setup automation. MCP canonical paths outside `repoRoot` (including symlink escapes) need explicit `allowOutsideRepo:true` after preview | Per section (dry-run first, `confirm:true` to write) |\n| Confluence/Notion/wiki page, via a third-party wiki MCP the user already registered (e.g. Atlassian's official Confluence MCP) | `/ontology-absorb-confluence` skill — that MCP reads the page (read-only), the returned markdown is fed into the same `absorb_document` pipeline, and the source page URL is cited in each landed node's body | Per section (dry-run first, `confirm:true` to write) |\n\nThe wiki path works identically for on-premise Confluence/wiki instances — the\nabsorption tool only ever reads a local markdown file; whatever gets it there\n(cloud MCP, on-prem export, `curl` to a file) is out of scope for this repo.\nThis project does not ship a Confluence integration; it ships an absorption\npipeline that a second, user-owned MCP can feed.\n\n### Interop — export to a standard graph format\n\nData flows *out* the same way it flows in: as portable files, no backend. The\nCLI `ontology-atlas export [vault] --format jsonld|graphml|json` compiles the\nvault (the deterministic `compile_ontology` artifact) and writes a standard\ninterchange format to stdout (status to stderr, so it pipes cleanly):\n\n- `jsonld` — RDF 1.1 JSON-LD; loads in rdflib / Protégé / any triplestore\n  (`g.parse('atlas.jsonld', format='json-ld')`).\n- `graphml` — XML graph; opens in Gephi / Cytoscape, loads via NetworkX\n  (`nx.read_graphml`) or Neo4j APOC (`apoc.import.graphml`).\n- `json` — the raw compile artifact unchanged (nodes/edges/`graphHash`).\n\nThe CLI `export` command emits JSON-LD/GraphML from this *same* serializer, kept\nbyte-identical by a contract test. (The web ERD builder that also consumed it was\nretired 2026-07-24 with the rest of `/ontology/edit`.) Node identity is the stable\n`urn:uuid:<uid>` (both the JSON-LD `@id` and the GraphML node id), while slug is\nexported as the readable current address. Contract: **an export is a snapshot**,\nthe compiler `graphHash` is its **version**, rename/reclassify preserve the URN,\nmerge preserves the survivor URN and absorbs source identities, and\nexternal/dangling refs are omitted\n(never phantom nodes). Full loading recipes live in `mcp/README.md` → *Interop*.\nRead-only MCP registration for external read consumers: set `OATLAS_READ_ONLY=1`\n(`tools/list` exposes only read tools; write calls are rejected).\n\nStaying file-only here is deliberate and matches the Obsidian precedent\n(files + offline core, servers behind an opt-in localhost plugin). A live HTTP\ntransport is out of scope until two concrete external-tool requests prove that\nfile export + the local stdio MCP genuinely can't serve them.\n\n**R14 — vault live updates** (`/topology` + all pages):\n\n- **Adaptive polling** (visible-only) — `useLocalVault` fingerprint check while the tab is visible; bursts to ~1.5s right after a detected change and decays to ~5s when idle, so agent / CLI writes surface fast without idle churn (generation-token poller avoids orphaned timers across hide/show)\n- **Graph diff pulse** — newly appearing slugs amber-pulse for 5s on `/topology`\n- **Toasts** — `Added: <slug>` (info) / `Edited: <slug>` (success, mtime change) on every page\n- **Save-conflict guard** — if a file changed on disk between read and write, `/docs` editor save surfaces a localized conflict notice and keeps the buffer dirty instead of silently overwriting unsaved edits\n- Effect: When files are edited via IDE · AI agent · CLI, the graph updates and toasts appear within ~1.5–5s without the user needing to click the web tab again.\n\n#### Read tools (19)\n1. **connection_info** — active vault/repo roots plus the actually advertised `readOnly`, `toolCount`, `toolNames`, and `toolsetHash`; explicit `OATLAS_REPO_ROOT` wins, otherwise repo root is auto-discovered from the active vault's Git top-level before falling back to process cwd\n2. **git_status** — vault-scoped working-tree state and risk; no writes or remote transport\n3. **git_history** `{ limit? }` — newest-first commits that touched the active vault pathspec only (default 20, max 100), with `limited` / `hasMore`, shallow-repository state, and `historyComplete` so truncated evidence is not mistaken for complete history\n4. **list_concepts** `{ kind?, domain?, since?, summary?, offset?, limit? }` — every node as `{uid, slug, …}`, optional filters, deterministic slug ordering, mtime, summary preview, and explicit `{returned, limited, pagination:{offset,limit,total,returned,hasMore,nextOffset}}` metadata for lossless large-vault traversal\n5. **get_concept** exactly one of `{ slug }` or `{ uid }` — full detail with both identities, frontmatter, prose, neighbors, edges, and `mtime`; UID lookup survives rename and never falls back to fuzzy matching\n6. **get_concepts** exactly one of `{ slugs }` or `{ uids }` — batch read (max 50), order-preserving partial results with both identities and per-node warnings\n7. **find_evidence** `{ title }` — partial-match across title / capabilities / elements / body; each match carries `{uid, slug}`, `domain`, `mtime`, and prose excerpt\n8. **find_backlinks** `{ slug }` — every referencing node as `{uid, slug, …}` (frontmatter arrays + wikilinks/markdown)\n9. **find_neighbors** `{ slug, direction?, types?, includeNodes?, limit? }` — one-hop local graph around a node, with canonical incoming/outgoing `edges[]` and `{uid, slug}` neighbor summaries (`includeNodes` defaults true, `limit` defaults 100/max 500); public relation type aliases like `depends_on` are normalized to stored graph keys\n10. **find_path** `{ from, to, maxHops? }` — shortest undirected BFS across graph frontmatter, including `domains` / `domain` containment (default 5 hops, includes aligned `{uid, slug}` `nodes[]` summaries plus `edges[via]`)\n11. **list_kinds** — vault kind census `{ total, byKind: { capability: N, … } }`\n12. **find_orphans** `{ kind?, excludeKinds? }` — isolated `{uid, slug}` nodes across graph frontmatter, including `domains` / `domain` containment (defaults exclude `project` and `vault-readme`; pass `excludeKinds: []` to include every kind)\n13. **query_concepts** `{ filter, limit? }` — typed filter DSL with AND/OR/NOT on `kind` / `domain` / `slug` / `title` / `has(arrayKey)`; match rows carry `{uid, slug}`\n14. **compile_ontology** `{ includeIndexes?, summary?, nodesLimit?, nodesOffset?, edgesLimit?, edgesOffset? }` — deterministic graph artifact with UID-required `nodes[]`, slug-based `edges[]`, identity indexes (`uidToSlug`, `slugToUid`, `mergedUidToSlug`), graph-array canonicalization actions, semantic `graphHash`, and pagination; invalid identity fails closed\n15. **query_ontology** `{ operation, ... }` — graph-engine query over the compiled artifact (`neighbors`, `path` with aligned `nodes[]`, `all_paths` with per-path `nodes[]` plus `limit` / `searchBudget` / `exhaustive` / `truncatedByBudget` / `totalPathsExact` metadata and `evidence` guidance, `query_plan` with executable run/narrow advice, filter-preserving `suggestedQuery`, and filter-aware `estimate.totalMatches` for `match_nodes` / `match_edges`, `centrality`, `communities`, `similar_nodes`, `explain_relation`, `reachability`, `pattern_walk`, `impact`, `blast_radius`, `subgraph`, `builder_context`, `overview`, `schema`, `facets`, `match_nodes`, `match_edges`, `node_profile`, `domain_profile`, `domain_matrix`, `project_scope`, `project_map`, `relation_check`, `components`, `lineage`, `containment_tree`, `cycles`, `topological_order`, `recommend_relations`, `growth_plan`, `maintenance_plan`, `agent_brief`, `workspace_brief`, `health`) for graph-database-like answers without pulling the full compile payload. `builder_context` keeps its compatibility operation/response name but emits the current Workshop focus URL, persisted bounded neighborhood, `canvasPosition`, `expected_mtime`, and safe low-level write handoff while declaring that unsaved UI drafts are not included. Repeated read calls inside one MCP server session reuse the compiled artifact while the vault document signature is unchanged, so first-contact agent run orders do not pay the full compile cost for every graph query. `match_nodes` returns a `followUp` packet for the first returned row with ready-to-run `node_profile`, incoming/outgoing `match_edges`, and `blast_radius` MCP calls plus CLI fallback commands, so a graph scan can become focused evidence without another round of tool-selection guesswork. `match_edges` returns a `followUp` packet for the first returned real edge with ready-to-run `explain_relation`, `path`, and `relation_check` MCP calls plus CLI fallback commands, so edge scans move directly into evidence and write-preflight instead of being treated as raw proof. `match_edges.filters`, `match_edges.edges[].relationType`, `followUp.focusEdge.relationType`, and `query_plan(match_edges).normalized` expose public names such as `depends_on` next to canonical frontmatter `types` or `via` values such as `dependencies`, so terminal and MCP clients can show the relation name users typed while keeping executable graph keys. `node_profile.edges.incoming/outgoing.byRelationType` and edge `relationType` expose public names such as `depends_on` for node detail views; `domain_matrix.filters.relationTypes`, `connections.rows[].byRelationType`, and connection examples do the same for coupling views, while canonical `types`, `via`, and `byRelation` stay available for graph-key callers. The UI semantic coupling matrix and CLI node deep dive can be rerun from Claude Code, Codex, or terminal fallbacks with the same user-facing names. `agent_brief` returns Claude Code/Codex handoff readiness, a copyable `handoffPrompt` (also printable via `ontology-atlas agent-brief --prompt`), graph entrypoints, first MCP calls, structured `graphDbQueryPack` (`facets` / `schema` / `query_plan(match_nodes)` / `match_nodes` / `query_plan(match_edges)` / `match_edges` / `domain_matrix` / `query_plan(centrality)` / `centrality` / `query_plan(all_paths)` / `all_paths` / `explain_relation` / `business_questions` outcome, domain-boundary, capability-claim, and implementation-evidence scans), investigation playbooks including `graph_traversal` (`schema` → `query_plan(all_paths)` → `all_paths` → `pattern_walk` / `project_map`), `traversalStrategy` (`plan_before_enumeration` → `bounded_path_evidence` → `containment_cross_check`) for plan-first bounded traversal, per-playbook `evidence[]` and `stopWhen[]` checklists, write guardrails for `add_relation` / rename-merge / post-change sync, relation preflight before `add_relation`, a `relationDecisionGuide` for the `skip_existing` / `review_inverse` / `safe_to_add` / `review_new_schema` outcomes, `resultContracts` requiring `all_paths` callers to report completeness fields and requiring `match_nodes` / `match_edges` callers to report `totalMatches`, `limited`, and `followUp` details before treating scan rows as evidence, and read-first write policy. The CLI companion `ontology-atlas agent-brief [vault] --graph-db-pack` turns that pack into a shell-pasteable graph scan script for sessions without MCP. `relation_check` validates relation `type` before endpoint slug resolution, so relation typos such as `depend_on` still return nearest-value hints even in empty or project-less vaults, and returns `matchingEdges`, reverse-direction `inverseEdges`, and a recommendation decision (`skip_existing`, `review_inverse`, `safe_to_add`, or `review_new_schema`). Non-dependency relations may expose an `add_relation` `proposedAction`; a new `depends_on` returns no executable args and instead exposes `approvalGate.writeAllowed:false` until observable ability, rationale, explicit human approval, and nonblank `why` are present. `maintenance_plan` actions include stable `id`, cursor resume via `afterActionId`, explicit `cursor.reason` metadata, executable graph-array canonicalization, count-safe summary fields, `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` remaining-queue buckets, `executable`, current-page `nextExecutableAction`, current-page `nextReviewAction`, plus `executableOnly` / `phases` / `severities` / `kinds` filters; ready pages report `cursor.found=true` with `cursor.reason=null`, while unknown cursors return an empty page with `cursor.found=false`, zero remaining actions, and no next actions. `phases`, `severities`, and `kinds` are enum-validated so typoed work-queue filters fail instead of returning an empty plan.\n`impact` and `blast_radius` follow only the `depends_on` relations that humans have explicitly written. Structural relationships such as what contains what are excluded from impact scope and risk calculations — for such structural questions, `reachability` and `subgraph` provide the answers. Each dependency edge is marked as either `review_required` (needs human review) or `declared_with_rationale` (reason provided), depending on whether a rationale is recorded. Until there is a current-source receipt confirming that each relationship remains factually accurate, the completeness and `risk` of this answer remain `unknown`.\n\n16. **validate_vault** — whole-vault health check with per-file issues and grouped summary, including required/valid/unique UID claims, merge identity history, graph-array canonicality, and dangling graph references\n\n`analyze_repo_structure`'s semantic discovery scans only up to 200 Markdown files and 1,000 directory entries across all three roots. General semantic documents stop reading at 256 KiB before being read. Visited real directories, archives, broken symlinks, or symlinks outside the repository do not expand the scan.\n\nDirect workspace members of `apps/*` and `packages/*` also become candidates for the same 6-document packet, including their static name+description `package.json` and package `README.md`. Only up to 48 members per conventional root are scanned; scripts/dependencies are not read, nor are package names automatically promoted to business meaning.\n\nBusiness capability candidates follow the same principle. They are proposed only when bounded outcome prose and implementation evidence are both confirmed; implementation-oriented folder names like UI, transport, policy, or telemetry are not automatically promoted to business meaning. Without evidence, they remain implementation review targets, and the analyzer does not write to the vault.\n\n17. **analyze_repo_structure** `{ rootPath?, maxDepth?, ignore?, proposal?, qualification? }` — side-effect-free bootstrap candidates from package / README / source layout plus the executable construction lifecycle. A valid complete proposal first returns an exact non-writing `reviewPlan`, plan/source digests, eight phase states, every `requiredGapId`, and a shadow-only `admission` receipt (`self_qualified`, `partial_visible_gap`, `human_review_required`, or `hard_block`); `self_qualified` is an auto-write candidate signal, not write permission. `canWrite` remains false and `writePlan` is absent until the existing human acceptance gate is satisfied. A separately identified evaluator then measures approved executive/employee/FDE/agent CQs, current claims/citations, seven quality axes, the complete source-hidden task, and cold-start/prior-CQ regression. After the user sees the exact plan and accepts its digest/revision plus every visible gap, the unchanged proposal and `constructionQualification:v1` packet may release a `writePlan` exactly equal to the reviewed rows. Maker-only evaluation, missing authority, `not_measured`, stale/private provenance, red mandatory axes, source/plan drift, regression failure, or an unaccepted gap fails closed. Acceptance is declared provenance, not authenticated identity or a truth certificate. Its five proposal competency answers still carry `answered` / `partial` / `visible-gap` plus typed concept, relation, evidence, and path witnesses, and the project body preserves that audit. `Excludes` is reserved for sourced product/concept boundaries: unknown or unmeasured evidence belongs in `Uncertainty` or a competency gap, and `epistemic-exclusion-boundary` blocks a proposal that would persist those unknowns as scope. Root `ARCHITECTURE.md` and classified Markdown under bounded `docs`, `site`, and `website` discovery can join the existing six-document semantic packet; archive-like paths and repository-escaping symlinks cannot. README extraction preserves purpose, responsibility/architecture, and ability blocks inside the existing 1,200-character budget instead of letting sponsor/backer/TOC sections consume it. Root package contracts remain bounded evidence, not meaning nodes: Rust reads allowlisted `Cargo.toml` package/features fields and returns separate literal `cfg`/`cfg_attr` provenance without evaluating predicates, executing code, or allowing relation writes. Python reads bounded static package evidence and import-participating boundaries; unused or unsafe inputs are skipped. Root Go modules contribute at most 24 import-participating package-directory element candidates, never path-derived capabilities. A proposal call recomputes the existing read-only import receipt so selectively proposed TS/JS/Python file endpoints and Go file/package endpoints are validated without relying on prior-call state, and import-backed `depends_on` must match observed direction. After the exact released rows land, the agent validates, compiles, connects the source, and finalizes project meaning.\n18. **infer_imports** `{ rootPath?, sourceFolders?, ignore?, maxFiles?, reviewMode?, afterReviewId? }` — side-effect-free TS/JS plus root-package Python file imports and root-module Go package imports. Existing file/module edges remain unchanged. Go is exposed separately as `packageImportEvidence` contract `goPackageImports:v1`: each row preserves the importing file, repository-relative source and target package directories, literal import spec, production/test role, and value usage without inventing a target file. It reads root-contained module-local imports only, never runs `go`, a compiler, module cache, or network, skips nested modules plus Go build-excluded `vendor`/`testdata`/underscore-prefixed fixture trees, ignores import-shaped lines inside multiline raw strings, caps files with the shared default 5000, caps each file at 256 KiB and 256 imports, and names external Go modules as out of scope. Its `coverage` receipt says which languages are supported; Cargo detection still marks Rust `use`/`mod`/macro dependency graphs unsupported. File and package receipts distinguish source role and usage; `value` does not claim runtime execution. Every collapsed edge includes whole-edge counts, their joint `productValueCount`, and up to five exact evidence receipts. Missing vault edges and Go package evidence are review-only, never executable write proposals. Compact and focus delivery surface Go counts plus the explicit full-evidence call instead of silently dropping a large package graph. CLI `infer-imports --apply` is disabled, and bootstrap/index cannot auto-create import endpoints or semantic `depends_on`; an agent must inspect both concepts, explain the meaning-level dependency, obtain human approval, and supply nonblank `why` before one explicit write.\n19. **index_project** `{ rootPath?, maxFiles?, threshold?, skipImports? }` — side-effect-free project indexing checkpoint that combines repo structure analysis, file-import and Go package-import indexing, and vault validation. It reuses one full import receipt for analyzer evidence, reports file and package relation counts separately, and preserves coverage instead of reducing uncertainty to one count. `plan.conceptDelta` separates raw candidates into existing, ambiguous-alias review, and genuinely new buckets, and `next.reviewCalls` gives exact calls for retrieving full rows before applying anything.\n\nFor `agent_brief`, structural readiness is not meaning confidence. A fresh call\nfor an explicit project derives `meaningAssessment:v1` from three independent\ndimensions: the current graph structure, the versioned competency receipt and\nits typed witness inventory, and project-source provenance/currentness. The\noverall result is categorical (`verified_current`, `needs_evidence`,\n`review_required`, or `invalid`); Atlas emits no combined score or percentage\nthat could hide a stale source or unresolved witness.\n\n`query_ontology({operation:\"cycles\"})` returns each cycle as the canonical slug\npath plus aligned `nodeSummaries[]`, so dependency-cycle diagnostics are readable\nwithout extra node lookups.\n\n#### Write tools (14)\n\nAll destructive dry-runs (`git_snapshot`, relation remove/replace,\nrename/reclassify/merge/delete, and absorb) expose the same agent decision\ncontract: `previewReady`, `canConfirm`, `wouldChange`, and\n`blockedReasons[]`. Tool-specific legacy `ok` is not the confirmation signal.\n\n1. **add_concept** `{ slug, kind, title, domain?, capabilities?, elements?, body? }` — create new `.md`; graph arrays are trimmed, deduped, and sorted on write (throws on existing slug); changed writes return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers\n   - **R6 validation**: title must be non-empty trimmed string (`isValidVaultTitle`)\n2. **add_concepts** `{ concepts }` — batch create nodes (max 50), order-preserving partial results; non-object row shape / unknown row field errors are isolated as `{ok:false, error}` rows, single unknown-field rows include `receivedField` plus one-row `unknownFields`, multi unknown-field rows report every offending field with nearest hints, and duplicate input slugs report both the failing `concepts[n]` row and first-seen `concepts[m]` via text plus structured `rowName` / `firstSeenAt`; changed batches return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers for the final graph\n3. **patch_concept** `{ slug, frontmatter?, body?, expected_mtime? }` — update existing; graph arrays are canonicalized, but immutable `uid` and merge-owned `merged_uids` cannot be changed by generic patch\n    - **R6 validation**: rejects `title: null` and `title: \"\"`\n    - **R11 conflict guard**: optional `expected_mtime` (from get_concept response). Throws `VaultConflictError` if file mtime differs at write time — caller re-reads and retries.\n4. **add_relation** `{ from, to, type }` — append to source frontmatter graph key; invalid relation `type` is rejected before endpoint slug resolution with a closest-value hint plus structured `valueName` / `receivedValue` / `suggestion` / `allowedValues`; changed writes return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers\n    - type enum: `depends_on` (→ `dependencies`) / `relates` / `contains` / `describes` / `domains` / `capabilities` / `elements` / `domain`\n    - **R7 validation**: both `from` AND `to` slug must exist in vault (`vaultSlugExists`)\n    - Unique tail aliases and frontmatter `slug:` aliases are resolved to canonical file slugs before write\n    - Idempotent: duplicate returns `{ alreadyExists: true }`\n5. **add_relations** `{ relations }` — batch edge writer (max 50), idempotent per row; non-object row shape / unknown row field errors are isolated as `{ok:false, error}` rows, single unknown-field rows include `receivedField` plus one-row `unknownFields`, multi unknown-field rows report every offending field with nearest hints plus structured `rowName` / `allowedFields` / `receivedFields`, and relation type typos include structured `valueName` / `receivedValue` / `suggestion` / `allowedValues`; stored relation arrays are deduped and sorted as canonical graph sets; changed batches return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers for the final graph\n6. **delete_concept** `{ slug, confirm?, force?, expected_mtime? }` — permanent delete; confirmed deletes return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers\n    - `confirm: false` (dry-run with backlinks preview) / `true` (actual)\n    - `force: false` (throw if backlinks exist) / `true` (delete anyway)\n    - **R11 conflict guard**: optional `expected_mtime`\n7. **rename_concept** `{ oldSlug, newSlug, confirm?, overwrite? }` — **R11** atomic graph-level rename\n    - Moves the .md file, updates the moved file's `slug:` key, rewrites every backlink (frontmatter array entries, inline string keys like `domain`, body links `[[oldSlug]]` / `(oldSlug.md)`)\n    - Tail-only references (`mcp-server` for `capabilities/mcp-server`) also redirected to the new tail\n    - `confirm: false` (dry-run with full update preview) / `true` (actual)\n    - Confirmed renames return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers\n    - Replaces the manual `find_backlinks` + N `patch_concept` loop\n    - Preserves the node UID; only the readable address and backlinks change\n8. **merge_concepts** `{ fromSlug, intoSlug, confirm?, expected_mtime?, expected_into_mtime? }` — **R11** atomic graph-level merge\n    - Redirects every backlink `fromSlug` → `intoSlug`, then deletes `fromSlug.md`\n    - Preserves `intoSlug` UID and records source identity history in canonical `merged_uids`; prose is not auto-combined\n    - For confirmed writes, pass both source and survivor mtimes so neither concurrent edit is overwritten\n    - `confirm: false` (dry-run) / `true` (actual)\n    - Confirmed merges return compact `postWriteMaintenance` with `byPhase` / `bySeverity` / `byKind` queue buckets, action `score`, executable `proposedAction`, and current-page next action pointers\n9. **remove_relation** `{ from, to, type, confirm?, expected_mtime? }` — one exact typed relation and its rationale, dry-run first; an absent relation is an explicit no-op blocker\n10. **replace_relation** `{ from, oldTo, oldType, newTo, newType, why?, confirm?, expected_mtime? }` — relation target/type/rationale replacement in one source-file write\n11. **reclassify_concept** `{ slug, newKind, newSlug?, domain?, body?, confirm?, expected_mtime? }` — kind/slug/domain transition with backlink redirect and generated-starter handling\n12. **absorb_document** `{ filePath, confirm?, allowOutsideRepo? }` — classifies a local agent-instruction document, writes accepted policy nodes, backs up the source, then rewrites it as a slim pointer. Canonical paths outside `repoRoot`, including symlink escapes, are blocked until a reviewed dry-run is repeated with `allowOutsideRepo:true`\n13. **git_snapshot** `{ confirm?, expectedHead?, message? }` — validates and commits only the active vault pathspec locally; blocks stale HEAD, detached HEAD, Git operations in progress, and validator errors; never pushes\n14. **finalize_project_meaning** `{ projectSlug, expected_mtime }` — post-write finalization for one explicit project. It reads the five competency answers from the current project Markdown; after current vault validation and a complete project scope, it resolves every typed witness against the current graph/source inventory and stores a versioned receipt with optimistic-concurrency protection. It stores no raw answers or private source coordinates. `ok: true` means the receipt write succeeded, not that the ontology or source is verified; callers read the returned categorical `meaningAssessment` or a fresh explicit-project `agent_brief`.\n\n---\n\n## 4. src/entities/docs-vault/data/content.json:16:  "FOUNDATIONS": "# FOUNDATIONS — what grounds ontology-atlas\n\n> This document ties the product to **public, citable academic/standard/craft references** rather than *feelings*.\n> A collection of grounds to prevent \"building without even knowing what ontology is\" — what already exists, and where/how we make *our own thing* differently on top of it.\n>\n> **Citation discipline:** All references cited here are public papers / W3C standards / public books / public blogs.\n> The initial set was re-verified with original text and official metadata on 2026-06-01, and the ontology-construction reinforcement set on 2026-08-09. Links/citations are provided, but the body text is not copied. When adding new references, maintain public, citable, and directly verified standards, and do not cite materials read only via search results.\n\nThis is a living document. When we make a design or feature decision, we should be able to point\nat *which* of these it descends from — or argue explicitly why we diverge.\n\n---\n\n## 1. What an ontology actually is\n\nThe word is older than software (Aristotle's *categories of being*), but our usage is the\n**information-science / knowledge-representation** one.\n\n- **Gruber (1993)** gave the most-cited definition: *\"an ontology is an explicit specification of a\n  conceptualization\"* — a representational vocabulary (classes, relations, functions, objects) for a\n  shared domain, designed so knowledge can be **shared and reused** across AI systems.\n  → Our vault's markdown frontmatter *is* \"an explicit specification of a conceptualization\" of a\n  codebase. The exact Atlas application model — five authorable kinds, one reserved reader kind,\n  relation support layers, `is_a` test, and inference boundary — lives only in\n  [`ONTOLOGY-ATLAS-SPEC.md` §2](ONTOLOGY-ATLAS-SPEC.md#2-the-five-authorable-node-kinds-and-reserved-reader-kind).\n  The name is earned by that shared meaning model, not by pretending the files implement a standard\n  they do not.\n- **Studer, Benjamins & Fensel (1998)** sharpened it to the canonical four-part definition:\n  *\"a **formal, explicit specification** of a **shared conceptualization**.\"* Word by word:\n  *conceptualization* = an abstract model of phenomena; *explicit* = concept types and constraints\n  are defined, not implied; *formal* requires a representation with defined semantics, not merely text\n  that a parser can read; *shared* = held in common rather than private.\n  → Atlas is explicit, shared, and machine-parseable. Its current Markdown schema does **not** claim\n  model-theoretic semantics, logical completeness, or a DL reasoner, so “machine-readable = formal” is\n  not our claim. This distinction is a trust boundary, not a downgrade.\n- **Noy & McGuinness, \"Ontology Development 101\" (Stanford, 2001)** is the practical methodology:\n  define classes + a hierarchy, define properties (slots) + constraints (facets), then instances —\n  and crucially, *\"ontology development is iterative, there is no single correct ontology, and the\n  right design depends on the intended application and anticipated extensions.\"*\n  → This is our **grow-the-vault-each-session, agent-maintained, no-one-true-model** stance, verbatim.\n\n### The formality spectrum — and where we deliberately sit\n\nThe W3C Semantic Web stack is the standard reference frame:\n\n- **RDF 1.1 (2014 Recommendation)** — RDF graphs are sets of subject-predicate-object triples whose\n  terms are IRIs, blank nodes, or datatyped literals. RDF 1.2 reached Candidate Recommendation Snapshot\n  on 2026-04-07; that work-in-progress status is not an endorsement or an Atlas compatibility claim.\n  An Atlas edge can be *mapped* to a triple-like statement, but the vault itself is not an RDF\n  serialization and does not inherit RDF identity or entailment semantics.\n- **OWL 2 (2012)** — the **heavyweight** end: classes/properties/individuals with **description-logic\n  reasoning** (consistency checking, classification, inference) under an open-world assumption. Atlas\n  does not adopt OWL vocabulary, class/individual semantics, or inference. Missing Atlas evidence is\n  `unknown`/a visible gap according to our application contract, not an OWL entailment result.\n- **SKOS (2009)** — the **lightweight** end: `skos:Concept` + `broader`/`narrower`/`related`.\n  `skos:broader` names a direct broader link and is not itself transitive; Atlas borrows that caution,\n  not SKOS semantics or conformance.\n- **SHACL 1.0 (2017 Recommendation)** — validates an RDF data graph against a separate shapes graph\n  and returns a validation report; it does not make OWL a closed-world schema language. SHACL 1.2 Core\n  was still a Working Draft on 2026-08-03. Atlas's validator plays an analogous product role over\n  Markdown, but it is an Atlas schema validator, not a SHACL processor.\n\n> **Our position on the spectrum:** a lightweight, application-specific ontology and executable\n> meaning model — more structured than tags, deliberately less expressive than RDF/OWL. Human-and-agent\n> readable Markdown, typed application relations, deterministic validation/query, no reasoner, no\n> backend. “Graph-shaped” describes the implementation; it does not assert standards conformance.\n\n### Construction is a requirements-and-tests lifecycle, not noun extraction\n\nThe literature converges on one discipline Atlas adopts: **start from the decisions the ontology must\nsupport, not from a directory tree or a list of nouns.** Grüninger & Fox make competency questions\nrequirements and benchmarks; NeOn and LOT put requirements, reuse, implementation, publication, and\nmaintenance in one lifecycle; SAMOD turns a motivating scenario, CQs, a glossary, exemplar data, and\nqueries into a regression-carrying test case.\n\nAtlas translates that lineage into an eight-stage, local-first construction contract:\n\n1. **Purpose and authority** — name the product outcome, intended users/decisions, scope, non-goals,\n   domain-language owners, and sources before proposing concepts.\n2. **Requirements as competency questions** — derive CQs from motivating scenarios; give each an\n   audience, expected answer shape, required witness kinds, explicit unknown/refusal behavior, and\n   owner approval. An LLM may draft a CQ, but may not approve its own requirement.\n3. **Evidence inventory and reuse** — separate direct, triangulated, structural, conflicting, and\n   absent evidence; search the existing vault before minting a term. A folder name is not a domain and\n   an import edge is not automatically a business dependency.\n4. **Small conceptual slice** — propose the smallest project→domain→capability→element slice that\n   answers a coherent CQ set. Give every concept an intensional definition, includes/excludes, examples,\n   counterexamples, and uncertainty. Do not expand the schema to fill a template.\n5. **Semantic and structural tests** — reject circular definitions, duplicate siblings, category\n   mistakes, dangling references, predicate-direction mistakes, and unsupported `is_a`. Same domain,\n   naming similarity, or folder nesting alone never proves subsumption.\n6. **Functional and pragmatic tests** — replay CQs against exemplar facts and expected answers, then\n   test whether a source-hidden person/agent can make the intended decision with bounded calls and\n   supported claims. A valid file is not necessarily a useful ontology.\n7. **Human acceptance and provenance** — persist only the accepted write plan; keep source spans,\n   graph/source digests, rejected/partial CQs, and the responsible human decision visible. Receipts are\n   provenance, not truth certificates.\n8. **Regression and evolution** — after each accepted change, rerun prior CQs, graph/schema validation,\n   source currentness, impact, and handoff checks. Git records change; the ontology still has to explain\n   why the meaning changed and which requirement authorized it.\n\nRecent LLM evidence makes the human-sovereign boundary stronger, not weaker. LLM-generated ontology\ndrafts can outperform novices in bounded studies, but quality remains variable; one 2025 CQ pipeline\nreported only about a quarter of outputs passing scope/relevance and fewer than half as unproblematic.\nThe 2026 IDEA2 workflow therefore separates LLM elicitation from domain-expert validation and records\nthe full CQ revision provenance. Atlas follows that separation: **agents accelerate elicitation,\nconstruction, and repair; people own meaning and accepted requirements; an independent evaluator owns\nqualification.**\n\n### Quality is a vector; no green total may hide a red dimension\n\nOQuaRE treats an ontology both as a software artifact and as a tool that must be useful. Atlas keeps\nthat separation and does not reduce construction quality to node count, fan-out, compiler health, or a\nsingle confidence score.\n\n| Dimension | Atlas question | Required evidence | Fail-closed result |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| Semantic correctness | Are kind, boundary, and predicate meanings defensible? | definitions, includes/excludes, examples/counterexamples, relation rationale | reject or `review_required` |\n| Structural conformance | Does the Markdown graph satisfy its declared schema? | parser/compiler/validator results, resolved references | block invalid writes/finalization |\n| Functional adequacy | Can it answer the approved CQs? | expected answer + quantified witness coverage | `partial` / `visible-gap` |\n| Evidence and provenance | Can each business claim be traced to current sources and an authority? | citations, source spans/digests, approval and receipt lineage | unsupported / stale |\n| Pragmatic usefulness | Can each audience make the intended decision without hidden source access? | source-hidden task result, claim ledger, time/calls | unknown / not-qualified |\n| Maintainability | Can a change be reviewed and prior meaning retested? | git diff, impact path, CQ regression, source-currentness check | maintenance action required |\n| Interoperability honesty | Are exports and standards claims limited to what is implemented? | declared format/profile and round-trip contract | no RDF/OWL/SHACL conformance claim |\n\nStructural metrics and automated judges are diagnostic signals, not acceptance authorities. OOPS! and\nOntoClean can expose modeling pitfalls; LLM graph judges can help triage noisy extraction; none replaces\ndomain requirements, exact witnesses, counterexamples, or independent task-level evaluation.\n\nThe re-executable evaluator packet, categorical verdict, privacy boundary, and representative fixture\nare specified in [Ontology Construction Qualification v1](ONTOLOGY-CONSTRUCTION-QUALIFICATION.md).\n\nFor Atlas, the conservative direct-subsumption test is executable prose, not a reasoner claim: both\nendpoints have the same `domain`/`capability`/`element` kind, every valid narrower example satisfies the\nbroader definition, the distinction is not synonymy or membership/part/dependency/sequence, and no known\naccepted concept fits between them. The normative rule and current `broader` write boundary live in the\nsame [meta-model contract](ONTOLOGY-ATLAS-SPEC.md#22-direct-is_a--broader-test).\n\n---\n\n## 2. Agent memory & LLM × knowledge-graph (the live field, 2023–2026)\n\nOur wedge — *\"the AI agent forgets the codebase every session; this is git-native ontology memory it\nmaintains and queries\"* — sits inside an active, recognized research lineage. We are **not** inventing\nthe category; we are taking a specific, opinionated position in it.\n\n**The \"LLM forgets; give it external memory\" premise:**\n\n- **MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023)** — \"virtual context management\": the model pages information between\n  a fixed context window (fast memory) and external stores (slow memory) via self-issued function\n  calls, simulating unbounded context. → We are the **codebase-specific, structured & human-readable\n  version of MemGPT's \"slow memory\"**: the agent pages the repo's mental model in/out through a runtime-advertised MCP surface\n  instead of opaque archival storage.\n- **\"A Survey on the Memory Mechanism of LLM-based Agents\" (Zhang et al., ACM TOIS, 2024)** — the\n  peer-reviewed taxonomy of memory *sources / forms / operations* and *evaluation*. → Lets us name our\n  choices precisely: **structured (KG) over textual** memory, **write-on-task-completion** operations,\n  **human-readable + git-versioned** storage, **codebase** domain. Safest single category-overview citation.\n\n**Memory as a maintained knowledge graph (the closest analogues):**\n\n- **Zep / Graphiti (Rasmussen et al., 2025)** — agent memory as a **temporal knowledge graph** with a\n  bi-temporal model (event time + ingestion time). The single closest published analogue to us: both\n  treat long-term agent memory as an explicit, maintained graph of typed entities + relations, not a\n  vector blob. → **Where we differ:** we get temporality *for free* from **git history + markdown\n  diffs** rather than a dual-timeline DB; our domain is the **codebase**, not conversation; our store\n  is **plain files in the repo**, not a graph DB.\n- **Mem0 (Chhikara et al., ECAI 2025)** — production memory with a plain-extraction mode *and* a\n  graph mode (`Mem0g`); emphasizes token-cost / latency savings from retrieving a small relevant slice\n  instead of full context. → Mirrors our choice to make **the graph the primary artifact** (markdown\n  frontmatter *is* the graph), and supplies our pragmatic argument: a maintained ontology lets the\n  agent fetch a small relevant subgraph instead of re-reading the whole repo each session.\n\n**LLM × KG more broadly:**\n\n- **Pan et al., \"Unifying LLMs and Knowledge Graphs: A Roadmap\" (IEEE TKDE, 2024)** — the canonical\n  framing of three patterns: KG-enhanced LLMs, **LLM-augmented KGs** (the LLM does construction /\n  completion / QA), and **synergized** LLM+KG as equals. KGs are positioned as *explicit, interpretable,\n  editable* stores that compensate for the LLM black box. → This *is* our core thesis. Our vault loop is\n  \"LLM-augmented KG + synergized\": the agent both **queries** the graph for grounding and\n  **maintains/extends** it.\n- **GraphRAG (Edge et al., Microsoft, 2024; + `microsoft/graphrag`)** — an LLM derives an entity graph\n  from documents, pre-summarizes communities, and answers *global* questions flat vector-RAG can't.\n  → The flagship example of an LLM **building and querying a graph as a memory/index layer**; we apply\n  the same pattern to a **codebase**. **Where we differ:** GraphRAG produces a generated artifact store;\n  our graph is a **human-editable, diff-reviewable markdown vault** that is the source of truth.\n- **\"LLMs on Graphs: A Comprehensive Survey\" (Jin et al., TKDE, 2023/2024)** — vocabulary for what we\n  are: a **text-attributed graph** (frontmatter nodes + typed edges) an LLM reasons over (as\n  predictor / encoder / aligner). Grounds the claim that LLMs *can* reason over typed-edge graphs, not\n  only prose.\n- **\"LLM-empowered Knowledge Graph Construction: A Survey\" (Bian, 2025, preprint)** — schema-based vs\n  schema-free KG construction, and explicitly names **\"dynamic memory for agentic systems\"** as a\n  direction. → Our per-kind normalized frontmatter schema is the schema-based pole; \"dynamic memory for\n  agentic systems\" is our exact positioning.\n- **\"Towards Agentic RAG with Deep Reasoning: A Survey\" (2025, preprint)** — \"agentic RAG\": an agent\n  loops over an external store to ground multi-step reasoning. → Frames our loop in current terms:\n  RAG-*enhanced reasoning* over a maintained graph, not one-shot retrieval.\n\n---\n\n## 3. The codebase side — code knowledge graphs\n\nThe other half of our lineage: representing **code** as a queryable graph rather than re-parsing it\neach time. The premise that a codebase's meaning is best captured as a graph of typed nodes + typed\nedges is well-established academic and industrial prior art.\n\n- **Code Property Graphs (Yamaguchi et al., IEEE S&P 2014)** — fuse AST + control-flow + program-\n  dependence into one queryable graph; express patterns as graph traversals (found 18 unknown Linux\n  vulnerabilities). → The foundational academic precedent for \"**a codebase's meaning is a unified\n  graph you traverse, not re-derive.**\" We fuse `project/domain/capability/element` + edges into one\n  vault the same way.\n- **Glean (Meta, open-source, 2024)** — schema-defined **typed facts** about code in a queryable fact\n  DB, interrogated with a Datalog-style language; powers navigation across a monorepo. → The closest\n  *industrial* analogue. **Contrast:** Glean = machine-*generated* facts; we = **human + agent-maintained,\n  git-native, markdown-as-source-of-truth.**\n- **SCIP (Sourcegraph, 2022)** — a portable, **human-readable**, language-agnostic code-index protocol\n  with stable string symbol IDs. → Validates our choice of a **portable, human-readable, on-disk**\n  representation (markdown frontmatter; slug-keyed nodes) over an opaque binary index.\n- **CodeQL (GitHub/Semmle)** — \"**treat code as data**\": extract a relational DB of facts, query it to\n  find patterns/variants. → The mainstream embodiment of \"**query your codebase like a database**\" —\n  precisely what we offer an agent via focused MCP graph queries (`find_path`, `find_backlinks`, …)\n  instead of\n  re-reading files.\n- **tree-sitter (Brunsfeld et al.)** — incremental parsing → concrete syntax trees with an\n  S-expression query system; the substrate beneath most code indexers (and our own CodeGraph index).\n  → The **structural** layer (\"what symbols exist, how they nest\"). We layer the **meaning** layer\n  (domains, capabilities, evidence, impact) *on top* — that separation is the point.\n\n> **The gap we fill:** CPG / Glean / CodeQL / tree-sitter answer *structural* questions\n> (what calls what, what's defined where) — machine-derived, exhaustive, regenerated. We hold the\n> **human-and-agent-meaningful** layer: *why* this exists, *which capability* it serves, *what breaks*\n> if it changes — curated (not exhaustive), maintained by the developer + agent together, in git.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Design lineage — restraint as craft, cited\n\nOur \"Linear-restrained\" design language (`docs/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md`, `.claude/rules/design.md`) is an\napplied reading of public, citable design thinking — not arbitrary taste.\n\n- **Dieter Rams, \"Ten Principles for Good Design\" (Vitsœ)** — *unobtrusive, honest, long-lasting,\n  thorough to the last detail,* and *\"as little design as possible\"* (\"Less, but better\").\n  → The rationale for neutral greys + a single indigo and the bans on glow/neon/gradients/glassmorphism.\n  Our whole forbidden-pattern list is applied Rams.\n- **Edward Tufte, *The Visual Display of Quantitative Information*** — **graphical integrity**\n  (representation proportional to the quantities) and **direct labelling** (a legend means the mark\n  cannot explain itself). → Grounds honest, proportional rendering of relations so agent and developer\n  read the *same true* model.\n  ⚠️ **The data-ink ratio is cited here as an aesthetic, not as our judgment rule** — it has been\n  tested and did not survive as one. Inbar, Tractinsky & Meyer (ECCE 2007) had 87 participants rate a\n  standard bar graph against its Tufte-minimalist twin and found a clear preference for the\n  non-minimalist version; Bateman et al. (CHI 2010) found embellished charts were described no less\n  accurately than plain ones and were recalled *significantly better* after two to three weeks.\n  Neither study touches graphical integrity, which is why that half stands. When a seat needs to\n  reject a mark, the rule it must cite is Mackinlay's expressiveness, below — \"this ink is not data\"\n  is an assertion those two papers can be pointed at, while \"this mark encodes no typed fact\" is not.\n- **Jock D. Mackinlay, \"Automating the Design of Graphical Presentations of Relational Information\"\n  (ACM TOG 5(2), 1986)** — **expressiveness** (a graphical language must encode the facts in the set,\n  *and no additional facts*) and **effectiveness** (given several expressive encodings, prefer the one\n  the human visual system reads best, ranking channels after Cleveland & McGill). → **This is the rule\n  the design bench actually runs**, and it is what the Infovis seat's mark → typed-fact table is: a\n  mark that maps to no fact fails expressiveness, and a mark that asserts a fact the data does not\n  contain (a decorative rail implying a category) fails it in the other direction. Effectiveness is\n  why `.claude/rules/design.md` sends bar identity to position/length/order/label rather than hue, and\n  why hue-only separation is a defect rather than a preference.\n- **Wathan & Schoger, *Refactoring UI*** (also the Tailwind authors) — establish hierarchy by\n  **de-emphasizing**, use a constrained spacing/type scale, **limit the palette deliberately**.\n  → The concrete how-to behind our `@theme` token scale, the per-screen gutter/spacing consistency\n  work, and the \"no second coloring system\" rule.\n- **John Maeda, *The Laws of Simplicity*** — *Reduce* and *Organize* (\"make a system of many appear\n  fewer\"); *\"subtract the obvious, add the meaningful.\"* → Justifies the kind hierarchy + typed\n  relations as the organizing device, and the agent's job of maintaining a **lean, high-signal** memory\n  graph rather than dumping everything.\n- **Karri Saarinen / Linear, \"Why is quality so rare?\"** — quality is a deliberate daily choice and a\n  strategic advantage; it spreads by advocacy, not ads; craft = believing it matters + skill to\n  recognize it + care for the user. → The canonical public statement of the philosophy our design\n  descends from — restraint as a *quality* decision that wins against louder AI-generated-UI clichés.\n- **Rauno Freiberg, \"Craft\" (rauno.me)** — exceptional UI is *invisible details* (microinteractions,\n  states, motion, polish) you feel, not flashy moments. → Our bar for hover/focus states, transitions,\n  and the topology's feel — *without* the forbidden flashy patterns.\n- **Emil Kowalski, \"Great animations\" (emilkowal.ski)** — natural physics-based motion; sub-300ms\n  ease-out; **purposeful** (convey state, not decorate); 60fps via transform/opacity only;\n  interruptible; respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. → Concrete, citable rules behind our motion budget\n  (`transition-colors`/opacity, sub-200ms, minimal transform). Justifies how the live topology animates\n  as the agent grows the vault: **state-conveying, not glow/pulse decoration.**\n- **Vercel Geist** & **Radix Primitives** — public reference points for the developer-tool aesthetic\n  (high-contrast accessible color, mono for code/diagrams) and the **\"unstyled accessible primitive +\n  our own theming\"** split we follow (inspector, forms, palette; the recent a11y label-association work).\n\n---\n\n## 5. Our own thing — what's genuinely ours\n\nEverything above already exists. Our contribution is a **specific combination** none of the prior art\nholds all of at once:\n\n1. **Agent-maintained** — the AI coding agent reads *and writes* the graph directly through the MCP server's runtime-advertised inventory,\n   not a human-only ontology editor (Protégé) and not a machine-only fact generator (Glean/CodeQL).\n2. **Git-native, markdown-IS-the-graph** — the frontmatter is the source of truth, reviewable as a\n   diff, versioned by git, no backend / no DB. (Zep/Graphiti = graph DB; GraphRAG = generated store;\n   mem0 = service. We = files in your repo.)\n3. **Live topology as the surface** — the same graph is the *human comprehension surface*: you watch it\n   grow as the agent edits, and you edit it back. (Mackinlay expressiveness + Linear's craft, applied to a KG.)\n4. **Codebase-scoped meaning layer** — not conversation memory (Zep/mem0) and not structural code facts\n   (tree-sitter/Glean), but the *why/owns/impacts* layer **on top of** structure, curated by developer +\n   agent.\n5. **Evidence-bound meaning receipts** — an agent can finalize five competency\n   answers, but the receipt is provenance, not an oracle. Every fresh project\n   brief rechecks the current graph, typed witnesses, and source receipt, and\n   keeps structural readiness, competency coverage, and source currentness as\n   separate categorical dimensions. This follows the same inspectability\n   principle as the vault itself: no combined confidence percentage can hide a\n   stale source or an unresolved witness.\n\n**The honest framing:** *agent memory = a maintained knowledge graph* (Zep, Pan et al., the memory\nsurvey all agree). We take the most **inspectable, lowest-infrastructure** position in that space — an\napplication-specific, graph-shaped meaning model that lives as Markdown in the repo, maintained by the\nagent and judged by the human. It is informed by ontology engineering and Semantic Web standards\nwithout claiming RDF/OWL/SKOS conformance. That is the thing to make excellent.\n\n---\n\n## References (public sources; initial set 2026-06-01, construction set 2026-08-09)\n\n**Ontology theory & standards**\n- Gruber, T. R.
